statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis as a teenager lowers IQ later in life, and the question is disputed. In a New Zealand birth cohort (Dunedin; 874 people analysed, born 1972-73; full-scale IQ tested at 7 to 13, when only 7 of 1,037 cohort members had tried cannabis, and again at 38; Meier et al., 2012), IQ rose by 0.05 standard deviations in the 242 people who never used cannabis (99.84 to 100.64) and fell by 0.38 (99.68 to 93.93, about 6 points) in the 38 people (about 4 in 100 of those analysed, editors' arithmetic; 82% men) who met criteria for cannabis dependence at 3 or more of 5 interviews between 18 and 38, with intermediate changes in between (linear trend t = −4.45, adjusted for sex). The trend held when people who had used cannabis in the day or week before testing, or had persistent tobacco, alcohol or hard-drug dependence or schizophrenia, were left out in turn, and after adjustment for education (t = −3.41), but its test statistic about halved (t = −2.20) when use in the past 24 hours, other dependence and schizophrenia were adjusted together, and no adjusted size or interval is reported. The decline was larger when dependence began before 18 (about −0.54 against −0.14 standard deviations at 3 or more interviews; 23 and 14 people; p = .02 by a test the paper does not describe, against p = .44 and .09 at 1 and 2 interviews, with no test of interaction); the 8 points that some reviews quote refer to these 23 people. A simulation by another researcher showed that differences in family socioeconomic status could produce the main pattern with no effect of cannabis, under assumed values (for example a fading schooling boost of about 4 IQ points for lower-status children), with the trend test significant at the 5% level in about half of 500 runs, though how often it produced a trend as strong as Dunedin's (P < 0.0001) is not reported (Rogeberg, 2013); in reply, the original team reported that family socioeconomic status did not significantly predict adolescent-onset dependence (P = 0.56) and was unrelated to IQ change (r = −0.006), and that the trend coefficient barely changed when socioeconomic status or childhood self-control was added, each on its own, or when only the 553 people from middle-class families were analysed (−0.152, then −0.158, −0.151 and −0.155; Moffitt et al., 2013). Two US twin cohorts with lighter, shorter use (ever use by 17 to 20 against never; 789 and 2,277 twins; subtests at 9 to 12 and again at 17 to 20) found that those who used changed by 4.0 and 3.4 points less on Vocabulary than those who never used, and by 2.0 points less on Information (−3.3 to −0.7; given in the larger cohort only), adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, socioeconomic status and cohort, but not on the four other subtests; in the larger cohort lower scores preceded use and the Vocabulary and Information differences shrank to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6) and −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9) after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (in the other cohort Vocabulary stayed at −3.7); and the twin who used did not differ significantly from the co-twin who did not (identical pairs −5.4, −11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs; −0.7, −3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs), with identical-pair intervals wide enough to include the between-family differences, although in the 99 non-identical pairs of the larger cohort the interval (0.2, −2.8 to 3.3) excluded that cohort's between-family difference of −3.4 (Jackson et al., 2016). In a British twin cohort (1,989 people tested at 5, 12 and 18), the 84 with cannabis dependence at 18 already had lower IQ at 5 and 12 (by 5.23 and 5.61 points, sex-adjusted), their IQ did not fall significantly more between 12 and 18 (−1.73 points, p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 0.9), and in 57 twin pairs in which only one twin was dependent, the twins did not differ at any age (Meier et al., 2018). The three Dunedin papers concern one cohort and count once; the twin cohorts studied mostly light use in late adolescence, while Dunedin studied dependence persisting into midlife. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: This has not been shown either way. In a New Zealand study, people who were dependent on cannabis at 3 or more of 5 check-ups between 18 and 38 (about 4 in 100 people in the study) lost about 6 IQ points from their childhood scores, while people who never used gained a little; the loss was larger when dependence began in the teens. Another researcher showed that differences in family background could produce a similar pattern; the original team found that family background (parents' jobs) did not change their result. In US and British twin studies of lighter teenage use, the twin who used did not lose clearly more IQ than the twin who did not, but these studies could miss a small loss and did not study years of heavy use. Researchers disagree.
population: People followed from childhood in population cohorts: New Zealand (Dunedin, born 1972-73, followed to 38), the United States (two twin cohorts, followed to 17-20) and England and Wales (E-Risk twins, born 1994-95, followed to 18)
exposure: Cannabis use in adolescence and early adulthood as each study defined it: DSM cannabis dependence at up to 5 interviews from 18 to 38, with onset before or after 18 (Dunedin); ever use by 17-20, 30 or more uses, or daily use for 6 months or more (US twins); past-year dependence or frequency at 18 (British twins); amount, potency and route not measured
comparator: Cohort members who never used cannabis (Dunedin; US twins) or were not dependent (British twins); in co-twin analyses, the co-twin who did not use or was not dependent
outcome: Change in IQ from before use (childhood or early adolescence) to 38, 17-20 or 18: full-scale IQ (Dunedin), Wechsler subtests in IQ points (US twins), IQ pro-rated from two subtests (British twins)
magnitude: Dunedin (Meier et al. 2012; IQ change in SD units, IQ points divided by 15, unadjusted group means; trend tests adjusted for sex): never used +0.05 (n = 242); used, never dependent −0.07 (479); dependence at 1 wave −0.11 (80), 2 waves −0.17 (35), 3 or more −0.38 (38; 99.68 to 93.93); trend t = −4.45, P < 0.0001; education-adjusted t = −3.41; multivariable (past-24-hour use, other dependence, schizophrenia) t = −2.20, P = 0.0282; no coefficients or intervals reported. Onset before against after 18 at 3 or more waves about −0.54 (n = 23) against −0.14 (n = 14), p = .02 by an undescribed test (p = .44 and .09 at 1 and 2 waves; bar heights read from a figure). Moffitt et al. 2013 (same cohort): β −0.152 (sex only), −0.158 (plus socioeconomic status), −0.151 (plus childhood self-control), −0.155 (553 from middle-class families); socioeconomic status and adolescent-onset dependence χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56; socioeconomic status and IQ change r = −0.006. Rogeberg 2013: simulation with no effect of cannabis, trend test significant at 5% in about 50% of 500 runs. Jackson et al. 2016 (ever use against never; IQ points; adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, socioeconomic status and cohort): Vocabulary −4.0 (−6.3 to −1.7; RFAB) and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3; MTFS); Information −2.0 (−3.3 to −0.7; MTFS only); with drinking and other drugs, Vocabulary −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5) and −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6), Information −0.7 (−2.3 to 0.9); co-twin Vocabulary, identical pairs −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5; 25 pairs) and −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4; 112 pairs), non-identical −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2; 54) and 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3; 99); 47 pairs discordant for heavy use −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6). Meier et al. 2018 (dependence at 18, 84 against 1,905; sex-adjusted IQ points): age 5 −5.23, age 12 −5.61, age 18 −7.34; change 12 to 18 −1.73 (p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 0.9); 57 discordant pairs, age 18 −1.45 (p = .42; approximately −5.0 to 2.1), change 0.05 (p = .98); frequency, change beta −0.05 (p = .035) in the full sample and −0.02 (p = .46) within pairs.

risk_of_bias.note: Dunedin and its reanalysis: confounding not addressed jointly (sex-only main models; socioeconomic status and self-control each added alone; the multivariable model's coefficient not reported) (cards sc_meier_2012, sc_moffitt_2013: ROBINS-E high). US twins: large missing data in one cohort (35% of eligible twins without exposure data, 41% of those analysed without follow-up testing; sc_jackson_2016, high). British twins: some concerns (sc_meier_2018). Rated down once for these problems.

inconsistency.note: Dunedin finds decline with persistent dependence; the three twin cohorts find no within-pair difference; within the US study, the two cohorts disagree on whether lower scores preceded use and on whether adjustment for other substance use removes the association.

indirectness.note: The studies test different exposures (dependence persisting into midlife against ever use by 17 to 20 or past-year use at 18) and different outcomes (full-scale IQ, Vocabulary and other subtests, IQ pro-rated from two subtests), so none answers the question for heavy teenage use with adult follow-up and a within-family comparison at once.

imprecision.note: Few people in the groups that carry the findings (38 with dependence at 3 or more waves and 23 with adolescent onset; 25 to 112 identical twin pairs; 57 discordant pairs), and the identical-pair co-twin intervals include both no difference and the between-family differences (the interval for the 99 non-identical pairs of the larger US cohort excludes it).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from four studies; not rated down.

large_effect.note: A loss of 0.38 SD in 38 people, without an adjusted estimate; no upgrade.

dose_response.note: Dunedin's decline grows with waves of dependence, but within one cohort, without a joint adjustment, and a gradient in a confounder could produce it; among people who used in the US twins, 30 or more uses or daily use did not go with significantly more decline (in the smaller cohort, intervals as wide as −4.5 to 3.7 points). No upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: Family and childhood factors would more plausibly create than hide the association; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on the causal question: the Dunedin association is a finding not in dispute, but whether cannabis caused it is, and the co-twin estimates are too imprecise to show that there is no effect. What the designs protect against: change scores from a childhood baseline remove stable differences between people, not influences that change over time; co-twin comparisons remove what twins share (all genes in identical pairs, about half in non-identical pairs, and the family environment), not factors that differ between twins, such as peers or other drug use, and the British study pooled identical and non-identical pairs. Overlap: Meier et al. (2012), Rogeberg (2013) and Moffitt et al. (2013) concern one cohort and count once (the simulation adds no data); the British twin study shares authors with the Dunedin team; the US study's two cohorts are independent of each other; the reviews (Broyd et al., 2016; Curran et al., 2016) describe these cohorts second-hand and add no data of their own; Curran et al. also relay a UK birth cohort (Mokrysz et al., 2016) that was not read for this answer. Status contested: credible evidence points both ways, and a published critique and reply disagree on how to read the same cohort.

debate.question: Does using cannabis as a teenager lower IQ later in life, or do other differences between people explain the lower scores?
debate.evidence_yes: In the only cohort here followed into midlife (Dunedin, New Zealand; Meier et al., 2012; sc_meier_2012; funded by public research councils in New Zealand, the UK and the US and a foundation; no conflicts declared), IQ was measured in childhood, before almost anyone had used cannabis, so stable childhood differences cannot explain the change scores. Full-scale IQ fell step by step with the number of interviews between 18 and 38 at which people met criteria for dependence, from +0.05 standard deviations in people who never used to −0.38 (about 6 points) in those dependent at 3 or more (trend t = −4.45), with significant downward trends on verbal and performance IQ and on four subtests; the trend held when people who had used in the day or week before testing, or had persistent tobacco, alcohol or hard-drug dependence or schizophrenia, were left out in turn, after adjustment for education (t = −3.41), and in a model adjusting for use in the past 24 hours, other dependence and schizophrenia together (t = −2.20, P = 0.0282). The decline was largest when dependence began before 18 (about −0.54 standard deviations, 23 people; p = .02 against adult onset at 3 or more interviews). When the socioeconomic explanation was tested in the cohort's own data, family socioeconomic status did not significantly predict adolescent-onset dependence (P = 0.56) and was unrelated to IQ change (r = −0.006), and adding it or childhood self-control, or analysing only the 553 people from middle-class families, left the coefficient essentially unchanged (−0.152 with sex only; −0.158, −0.151 and −0.155) (Moffitt et al., 2013; sc_moffitt_2013; written by the original authors; no conflicts declared). In the US twin cohorts, the between-family Vocabulary decline remained after adjustment for socioeconomic status, and in one cohort after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (−3.7, −6.8 to −0.5); the identical-twin estimate in that cohort (−5.4, −11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs) points towards harm and is larger than the between-family difference (Jackson et al., 2016; sc_jackson_2016). In the British twins, more frequent use went with a slightly greater IQ decline in the full sample (−0.05 standard deviations per standard deviation of frequency, p = .035; Meier et al., 2018; sc_meier_2018). The authors of both twin studies note that their participants were young and mostly used lightly, so effects of years of heavy use cannot be ruled out.
debate.evidence_no: Change scores remove stable childhood differences, not influences that act over time. A simulation in which family socioeconomic status shapes both cannabis exposure and IQ change, with no effect of cannabis at all, produced group means like Dunedin's main table, with the trend test significant at the 5% level in about half of 500 runs (how often it produced a trend as strong as Dunedin's is not reported) (Rogeberg, 2013; sc_rogeberg_2013; funded by the Norwegian Research Council; no conflicts declared); the reply did not report the joint model with several childhood factors, or the IQ trajectories before use by later exposure group, that this critique proposed. In two US twin cohorts (Jackson et al., 2016; sc_jackson_2016; funded by the US National Institutes of Health; no conflicts declared), twins who used cannabis did not decline more than their co-twins who did not, in identical or non-identical pairs (for example −0.7, −3.9 to 2.4, in 112 identical pairs, and 0.2, −2.8 to 3.3, in 99 non-identical pairs, an interval that excludes the between-family difference of −3.4), nor in 47 pairs in which one twin used heavily (−1.5, −5.5 to 2.6); in the larger cohort, lower Vocabulary, Information and Block Design scores at 11 to 12 already preceded use, and the Vocabulary difference shrank from −3.4 to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6) once drinking and other drug use were taken into account; among people who used, 30 or more uses or daily use did not go with significantly more decline. In a British twin cohort followed from 5 to 18 (Meier et al., 2018; sc_meier_2018; funded by the UK Medical Research Council and others; no declaration of interests in the author manuscript), adolescents with cannabis dependence at 18 already had IQs about 5 points lower at 5 and at 12, did not lose significantly more IQ between 12 and 18, and did not differ from their non-dependent co-twins at any age (57 pairs; at 18, −1.45, p = .42), which the authors read as family background explaining the lower scores. A narrative review relays a UK birth cohort of 2,235 adolescents aged 15–16 in which cumulative use was not linked to lower IQ once pre-teen IQ and confounders, notably tobacco and alcohol use, were taken into account, though only 72 reported more than 50 uses (Curran et al., 2016, Box 1; second-hand, the study itself not read). In Dunedin itself, the test statistic about halved when other dependence and use in the past 24 hours were adjusted together, no adjusted size is reported, the adolescent-onset contrast rests on 23 and 14 people without a test of interaction, and 3 of 7 IQ subtests showed no decline in the most persistent group (Meier et al., 2012).
debate.neither_can_show: No study here combines the three things the question needs: heavy, persistent use from adolescence; IQ measured before use and again in adulthood; and a comparison within families. Dunedin has the first two but not the third, and its most exposed group is 38 people; the twin studies have the second and third, but their exposure (mostly ever use by 17 to 20, or light past-year use at 18) is far lighter and shorter, so their null results and Dunedin's decline do not answer the same question. Co-twin comparisons remove the genes and family environment that twins share (all genes in identical pairs, about half in non-identical pairs, which the British study pooled), not differences between twins in peers, behaviour or other drug use, and their intervals cannot exclude declines of a few points. Adjusting for education, drinking or other drug use removes confounding if these are causes of both, but removes part of a real effect if cannabis use leads to them; the data cannot tell which. All exposure was self-reported, potency was not measured, and recent use before testing was not recorded in the twin studies. Reviews quote the Dunedin decline as up to 6 or around 8 points: about 6 is the group dependent at 3 or more interviews (38 people), and 8 the subgroup whose dependence began before 18 (23 people).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In one New Zealand cohort, the 38 of 874 people (about 4 in 100) with cannabis dependence at 3 or more interviews from 18 to 38 lost about 6 IQ points relative to their childhood scores, while people who never used held steady, and two named confounders, family socioeconomic status and childhood self-control, each tested alone, did not explain this. In twin studies of lighter use ending at 18 to 20, lower scores were partly present before use and did not differ between twins, which points to family factors behind much of the difference at those ages; but these studies cannot exclude a decline of a few points and do not test years of heavy use. The evidence does not show that teenage cannabis use lowers later IQ, nor that it does not: it fits both a modest effect of long, heavy use that begins in adolescence and confounding by factors that change over time.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A large cohort that tests IQ, memory and executive functions before any use and repeatedly from adolescence into adulthood, records frequency, potency and recent use at each wave with biological checks, follows enough people with persistent heavy use, and compares twins or siblings who differ in use while adjusting jointly for family socioeconomic status, self-control, conduct problems, other drug use and family psychiatric history, with effect sizes, intervals and a margin for no effect stated in advance. In the Dunedin data, two analyses proposed in the published critique would test the confounding model directly: IQ trajectories across the childhood tests by later exposure group, and one model with the childhood factors together. Later analyses in the project's lists (the Dunedin follow-up at 45; co-twin analyses by Schaefer and colleagues; a UK birth cohort, Mokrysz and colleagues) were not read for this answer.
